questions.q: What does CAP theorem actually claim, precisely, according to this lesson?
options: A distributed system can't fully guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance all at once, and the claim really only bites during a partition
A distributed system can never be both consistent and available under any circumstances
CAP theorem applies only to single-machine, non-distributed databases
CAP theorem guarantees all three properties as long as the system uses enough servers
questions.explain: Outside of an actual network partition, a well-built system can often approach all three properties.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say CAP effectively reduces to a choice between C and A, not a genuine choice among all three?
options: Because partition tolerance isn't optional — any real distributed system will eventually hit a partition, so the only real decision is what happens when it does
Because partitions never actually happen in real systems
Because availability and consistency are actually the same property
Because partition tolerance is always sacrificed first in every design
questions.explain: A partition is a fact about distributed systems, not a design choice you can decline — so the real question is C vs. A when it happens.

questions.q: What does a CP-leaning system do during a network partition, per this lesson's example?
options: It would rather block or error than let a client read an inconsistent balance from a single-writer transactional source
It always returns a response no matter what, even if the data might be stale
It shuts down permanently until the partition is manually resolved
CP systems ignore partitions entirely
questions.explain: CP favors correctness over availability during a partition — refusing to answer rather than risk showing bad data.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe the fraud-detection case study (Lesson 21) as leaning AP on purpose?
options: Because it's usually better to score a transaction with slightly stale features than to block or error out during a network hiccup
Because fraud detection has no relationship to distributed systems trade-offs
Because AP systems are always faster than CP systems in every scenario
Because fraud detection requires perfectly consistent data at all times
questions.explain: A transaction-scoring system generally shouldn't hang during a partition — availability matters more than perfect freshness here.

questions.q: What is the honest, practical takeaway this lesson gives about applying CAP theorem in real system design?
options: Real systems rarely sit at a pure extreme, and the useful question is what happens during a partition for this specific read path and consumer
CAP theorem should be applied as one binary, system-wide choice and never revisited per operation
CAP theorem has no practical use in real data engineering work
Every distributed system must choose availability over consistency, always
questions.explain: Systems like Delta Lake and Cosmos DB offer tunable consistency per operation — the theorem hands you a question to ask, not an answer.
